learning.title: Cite an artifact only when you can name the command that produced it at this head
learning.trigger: Citing a file as evidence for a property of the current branch: a parity report, a green test summary, a stored capture, a screenshot set, a queue state, an approval.
learning.mistake: An artifact is read as if it were a measurement of the claim, when it is downstream of some earlier run. Four faces of one move in one day. A parity report graded a branch against artifacts/ui-baseline/runtime/manifest.json, which was a gitignored symlink to another worktree's capture at an unrelated commit and an older schema; the report's "359 passed" was true of the pixels it compared and false of the branch. A QA tick rested on a readback true when read and false a minute later. A byte-order theory was inferred from the shape of two failures. A test asserted an ordering derived from the ids it happened to observe. In each case the artifact sat downstream of the property being claimed: a manifest is downstream of a capture, the branch's rendering is upstream of it. A stale artifact lies by omission; the worse shape is the wrong instrument, which lies by destruction - a capture run chosen for a job that did not need a database wrote the site case set over the auth candidate it was meant to measure, and the two sets shared no case ids at all.
learning.rule: Before citing an artifact, answer two questions in one line each: can I name the command that produced this, and did I run it in this session at this head? If either answer is no, the artifact is a claim about some other moment and must not carry the current head's name. Prefer the checks that build their own inputs (fixture-based tests, re-runnable comparisons) over the reports that consume someone else's output. A resource constraint that looks inapplicable to the job is a signal to re-read which job it belongs to, not a licence to bypass it: the wrong-instrument run above was justified by reasoning about a database the capture never touched, and the gate was right while the model of the work was wrong. When a downstream artifact is genuinely the only evidence, say which earlier run produced it and at which revision, and keep it out of the head's evidence block. Repair a known-stale artifact in place rather than annotating it: delete or replace the symlink so the stale read becomes impossible and the next run fails loudly, because a comment saying "this may be stale" is the same refusal-to-repair as a note that hides a stale SHA.

verification.requirement: The artifact path resolves to a real directory, and the identity the gate actually compares recomputes from the commit under test: compare-paper.mjs checks the per-profile digest and never reads the candidate's recorded sourceCommit, so naming that field would itself cite something downstream of the property. A report whose candidate manifest is missing or dates from another worktree fails loudly instead of grading stale pixels.
